items.stem: An e.m.f. is induced in a wire when
options: the wire is held still in a steady field
a current is switched off in a different room
the wire cuts magnetic field lines
items.answer: the wire cuts magnetic field lines
items.markingKey: Induction needs relative movement or a changing field linked to the conductor.

items.stem: A magnet is held stationary inside a coil connected to a meter. Explain why the meter reads zero.
items.answer: No field lines are being cut / the field through the coil is not changing, so no e.m.f. is induced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: A magnet’s north pole is pushed into a coil. Explain, using Lenz’s law, what pole forms at that end of the coil.
items.answer: A north pole forms, which repels the incoming north pole, opposing the change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: north; 1 mark: opposes motion.

items.stem: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Predict what happens if the magnet is pushed in twice as fast, and explain.
items.answer: Larger deflection (about double), same direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (rate of cutting field lines / direction of change).

items.stem: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Predict what happens if the magnet is pushed in with the south pole first, and explain.
items.answer: Same size deflection in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (rate of cutting field lines / direction of change).

items.stem: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Predict what happens if the magnet is pushed in and then held still, and explain.
items.answer: Deflection while moving, then zero once the magnet stops.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (rate of cutting field lines / direction of change).

items.stem: A small wind turbine drives a coil that rotates 25 times per second in a magnetic field. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) Describe how the output voltage–time graph changes if the speed doubles.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Peaks twice as high and twice as many cycles per second.

items.stem: A model a.c. generator has a coil rotating 25 times per second between two magnets. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) Describe how the output voltage–time graph changes if the speed doubles. (c) State the purpose of the slip rings.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Peaks twice as high and twice as many cycles per second. (c) They keep the rotating coil connected to the external circuit so the output stays a.c.

items.stem: Which change increases the e.m.f. induced when a magnet is pushed into a coil?
options: Holding the magnet still inside the coil
items.answer: Moving the magnet faster
items.markingKey: Faster motion, stronger magnet or more turns increases the e.m.f.

items.stem: The direction of an induced current is always such that it
options: is the same as the field direction
items.answer: opposes the change producing it
items.markingKey: Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change that causes it.

items.stem: Explain why pulling a magnet out of a coil gives a meter deflection in the opposite direction to pushing it in.
items.answer: The change in the field is reversed, so the induced e.m.f. (and current) is reversed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a voltmeter. The speed of the magnet is doubled while the number of turns on the coil stays the same. Explain how the induced e.m.f. changes.
items.answer: The induced e.m.f. doubles.
items.markingKey: Using induced e.m.f. ∝ rate of change of magnetic field: induced e.m.f. ∝ speed of the magnet; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Predict what happens if the magnet is pushed in with a coil of twice as many turns, and explain.
items.answer: Larger deflection (about double), same direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason (rate of cutting field lines / direction of change).

items.stem: A coil is connected to a galvanometer and a magnet is moved in and out of it. Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows.
items.answer: The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed.

items.stem: A coil is connected to a galvanometer and a magnet is moved in and out of it. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) Describe what the meter shows when the magnet is held still inside the coil.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) Zero: no change in field, no e.m.f.

items.stem: A small wind turbine drives a coil that rotates 50 times per second in a magnetic field. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced. (b) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows. (c) State the frequency of the a.c. output. (d) State the purpose of the slip rings.
items.answer: (a) The coil cuts / experiences a changing magnetic field. (b) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed. (c) 50 Hz (d) They keep the rotating coil connected to the external circuit so the output stays a.c.

items.stem: In an a.c. generator, what are slip rings used for?
options: To keep a continuous connection between the rotating coil and the external circuit
To increase the speed of rotation
To reverse the current every half turn
items.answer: To keep a continuous connection between the rotating coil and the external circuit
items.markingKey: Slip rings and brushes connect the spinning coil to the circuit without twisting wires; the output stays alternating.

items.stem: Explain why the output of an a.c. generator reverses direction every half turn.
items.answer: Each side of the coil moves up then down through the field, so the direction of cutting reverses.

items.stem: Explain why the output of a generator is zero when the coil is perpendicular to the field.
items.answer: At that instant the coil sides move parallel to the field lines, so no lines are cut.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 50 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is halved. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 50 Hz (b) frequency becomes 25.0 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is halved as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 5 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is halved. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 5 Hz (b) frequency becomes 2.50 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is halved as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: A coil is connected to a galvanometer and a magnet is moved in and out of it. (a) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (b) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows.
items.answer: (a) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (b) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed.

items.stem: The e.m.f. of an a.c. generator is greatest when the plane of the coil is
items.answer: parallel to the magnetic field
items.markingKey: Coil sides then cut field lines fastest.

items.stem: Compare the a.c. generator and the d.c. motor in terms of energy changes.
items.answer: Generator: kinetic → electrical; motor: electrical → kinetic.

items.stem: Explain why slip rings, not a split-ring commutator, are used in an a.c. generator.
items.answer: Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same brush, so the output alternates.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 60 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is doubled. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 60 Hz (b) frequency becomes 120 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is doubled as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 25 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is halved. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 25 Hz (b) frequency becomes 12.5 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is halved as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: A model a.c. generator has a coil rotating 10 times per second between two magnets. (a) State two ways of increasing the induced e.m.f. (b) Use Lenz's law to explain why there is a force opposing the motion when current flows.
items.answer: (a) Move/rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns (any two). (b) The induced current produces a field that opposes the change/motion, so extra work is needed.

items.stem: A step-up transformer has
options: more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary
fewer turns on the secondary coil
items.answer: more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary
items.markingKey: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; step-up means Ns > Np.

items.stem: A laptop charger contains a transformer. The number of secondary turns is doubled while the number of primary turns stays the same. State and explain how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage doubles.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of secondary turns; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A laptop charger contains a transformer. The number of primary turns is increased by 50% while the number of secondary turns stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage falls to two thirds.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of primary turns^-1.00; factor = 1.50^-1.00 = 0.667. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A transformer has 1000 turns on the primary and 40000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 400,000 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
A transformer has 4000 turns on the primary and 8000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 11,000 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 22,000 V; step-up

items.stem: A transformer has 2000 turns on the primary and 10000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 120 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 600 V; step-up

items.stem: A power station sends 2.0 × 10⁷ W along cables of total resistance 5 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 11,000 V and at 275,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 11,000 V: I = 1820 A, loss = 1.65 × 10⁷ W. At 275,000 V: I = 72.7 A, loss = 2.64 × 10⁴ W. Raising V by ×25.0 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×625).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: A power station sends 1.0 × 10⁷ W along cables of total resistance 5 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 20,000 V and at 132,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 20,000 V: I = 500 A, loss = 1.25 × 10⁶ W. At 132,000 V: I = 75.8 A, loss = 2.87 × 10⁴ W. Raising V by ×6.60 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×43.6).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: Why do transformers only work with alternating current?
options: Direct current would melt the core
Alternating current has a higher voltage
Direct current cannot pass through copper
A changing magnetic field is needed to induce an e.m.f. in the secondary coil
items.answer: A changing magnetic field is needed to induce an e.m.f. in the secondary coil
items.markingKey: Direct current gives a steady field, so no e.m.f. is induced.

items.stem: A transformer powers a model railway. The number of secondary turns is halved while the number of primary turns stays the same. Explain how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage halves.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of secondary turns; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Explain why transformers become warm in use.
items.answer: Some energy is wasted heating the coils (resistance) and the core (eddy currents).

items.stem: A laptop charger contains a transformer. The number of primary turns is multiplied by 5 while the number of secondary turns stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage falls to one fifth.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of primary turns^-1.00; factor = 5.00^-1.00 = 0.200. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A transformer at a substation has a primary voltage of 240 V. The turns ratio Np : Ns is 800 : 20. Explain why the transformer would not work with a d.c. supply.
items.answer: A steady current gives a constant field; no change in field so no e.m.f. induced.

items.stem: A phone charger transformer steps 120 V down to 9 V and supplies a current of 2.50 A to the phone. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate the current in the primary coil.

A transformer has 500 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary is connected to a 25,000 V a.c. supply. (a) State whether it is a step-up or step-down transformer. (b) Explain how an e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil.
items.answer: (a) step-down (b) Alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which links the secondary and induces an e.m.f.

items.stem: A power station sends 2.0 × 10⁷ W along cables of total resistance 8 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 20,000 V and at 132,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 20,000 V: I = 1000 A, loss = 8.00 × 10⁶ W. At 132,000 V: I = 152 A, loss = 1.84 × 10⁵ W. Raising V by ×6.60 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×43.6).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: Which equation gives the power lost as heat in a transmission cable?
items.answer: P = I²R
items.markingKey: Heating loss depends on the square of the current.

items.stem: Explain why the national grid uses step-up transformers at power stations and step-down transformers near homes.
items.answer: Stepping up the voltage reduces the current for the same power, reducing I²R heating losses in the cables; stepping down makes the voltage safe for homes.

items.stem: Explain why thicker transmission cables reduce energy loss but are not always used.
items.answer: Thicker cables have lower resistance so less I²R loss, but they are heavier and more expensive, needing stronger pylons.

items.stem: A power station sends 5.0 × 10⁶ W along cables of total resistance 4 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 25,000 V and at 400,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 25,000 V: I = 200 A, loss = 1.60 × 10⁵ W. At 400,000 V: I = 12.5 A, loss = 6.25 × 10² W. Raising V by ×16.0 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×256).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: A power station sends 2.0 × 10⁷ W along cables of total resistance 10 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 25,000 V and at 400,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 25,000 V: I = 800 A, loss = 6.40 × 10⁶ W. At 400,000 V: I = 50.0 A, loss = 2.50 × 10⁴ W. Raising V by ×16.0 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×256).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.

items.stem: An engineer tests a transformer: primary 230 V a.c., 1000 turns; secondary 40 turns. (a) Calculate the output voltage. (b) Explain why the core is made of soft iron.
items.answer: (a) 9.20 V (b) It is easily magnetised and demagnetised, concentrating the changing field to link both coils.
items.markingKey: (a) Vs = Vp × Ns/Np [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Electricity is sent along overhead cables. The current in the cables is halved while the resistance of the cables stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the power lost in the cables changes.
items.answer: The power lost in the cables becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power lost in the cables ∝ current in the cables^2.00; factor = 0.500^2.00 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Compare the a.c. generator and the d.c. motor in terms of energy changes. (b) Explain why slip rings, not a split-ring commutator, are used in an a.c. generator.
items.answer: (a) Generator: kinetic → electrical; motor: electrical → kinetic. (b) Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same brush, so the output alternates.

items.stem: A coil in a generator turns 50 times per second. (a) State the frequency of the output. (b) The speed of rotation is doubled. Describe two changes to the output graph.
items.answer: (a) 50 Hz (b) frequency becomes 100 Hz and the peak e.m.f. is doubled as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: f = rotations per second; 1 mark: new frequency; 1 mark: peak voltage changes the same way.

items.stem: A small wind turbine drives a coil that rotates 25 times per second in a magnetic field. (a) State the frequency of the a.c. output. (b) Describe how the output voltage–time graph changes if the speed doubles. (c) State the purpose of the slip rings.
items.answer: (a) 25 Hz (b) Peaks twice as high and twice as many cycles per second. (c) They keep the rotating coil connected to the external circuit so the output stays a.c.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A step-up transformer has (b) Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltages?
items.answer: (a) more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary (b) To reduce the current and so reduce energy lost as heat in the cables
items.markingKey: (a) Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; step-up means Ns > Np. (b) P = IV: for the same power, higher V means lower I; loss = I²R.

items.stem: A laptop charger contains a transformer. The number of secondary turns is multiplied by 5 while the number of primary turns stays the same. State and explain how the output voltage changes.
items.answer: The output voltage becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using Vs/Vp = Ns/Np: output voltage ∝ number of secondary turns; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 40000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 11,000 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 880,000 V; step-up

items.stem: An engineer tests a transformer: primary 25,000 V a.c., 500 turns; secondary 50 turns. Explain why the core is made of soft iron.
items.answer: It is easily magnetised and demagnetised, concentrating the changing field to link both coils.

items.stem: A transformer has 400 turns on the primary and 40000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 120 V. Calculate the secondary voltage and state whether it is step-up or step-down.
items.answer: 12,000 V; step-up

items.stem: A transformer at a substation has a primary voltage of 25,000 V. The turns ratio Np : Ns is 1000 : 20. (a) State whether it is a step-up or step-down transformer. (b) Explain how an e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil. (c) Explain why the transformer would not work with a d.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) step-down (b) Alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which links the secondary and induces an e.m.f. (c) A steady current gives a constant field; no change in field so no e.m.f. induced.

items.stem: A village is supplied through a long cable. The resistance of the cables is doubled while the current in the cables stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the power lost in the cables changes.
items.answer: The power lost in the cables doubles.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power lost in the cables ∝ resistance of the cables; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A wind farm sends power to the grid along underground cables. The resistance of the cables is multiplied by 5 while the current in the cables stays the same. Explain how the power lost in the cables changes.
items.answer: The power lost in the cables becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power lost in the cables ∝ resistance of the cables; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A power station sends 5.0 × 10⁶ W along cables of total resistance 4 Ω. Compare the power lost in the cables if it is transmitted at 20,000 V and at 132,000 V, and explain the result. Assume the transformers are 100% efficient.
items.answer: At 20,000 V: I = 250 A, loss = 2.50 × 10⁵ W. At 132,000 V: I = 37.9 A, loss = 5.74 × 10³ W. Raising V by ×6.60 cuts I by the same factor and loss by its square (×43.6).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each current (I = P/V); 1 mark each loss (P = I²R); 1 mark explanation of square law.
